# Prikk installer (Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7).
#
# Generated by `prikk-release-policy generate-installer` at release time and published as a
# release asset (never committed as a tracked .ps1 file) -- see docs/src/guide/install.md.
#
# A passing checksum here proves this download matches what the release page published; it does
# not prove *who* published it. In v0 one maintainer key signs every release tag; release-signers.toml
# is empty because no multi-signer policy exists yet -- see the release, versioning, and compatibility
# reference for the full statement. This script never claims more than that.
#
# Usage (the one-line form; code piped to Invoke-Expression is not subject to execution policy,
# unlike a saved .ps1 file run directly -- see docs/src/guide/install.md for the downloaded-file
# form and what to do about execution policy there):
#   irm https://github.com/REPO_SLUG/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
#
# Environment overrides (there are no --version/--prefix flags here, unlike install.sh: the
# one-line `irm | iex` form has no way to forward positional arguments the way `sh -s --
# --version X.Y.Z` does, so environment variables are the only override this script supports):
#   PRIKK_INSTALL_VERSION   version tag to install, default "latest"
#   PRIKK_INSTALL_DIR       install directory, default "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\prikk"
#   PRIKK_INSTALL_BASE_URL  override the download base URL (undocumented, test-only)
#
# Windows installer/uninstaller handoff v1 Part 6a2 (review 0.54.0-step-3-part-6a-review-v1,
# condition C1): the entire body below is wrapped in one script block invoked once with the call
# operator (`& { ... }`). `about_Operators`'s own Call operator section states plainly: "The call
# operator executes in a child scope" -- and `about_Scopes` states the general rule a child scope
# follows: "Items that you create or change in a child scope don't affect the parent scope, unless
# you explicitly specify the scope when you create the items." Confirmed from both pages before
# relying on it, not assumed. That is what makes this safe to run as `irm ... | iex`: today,
# `$ErrorActionPreference` and every working variable ($repo, $version, $installDir, $workDir, ...)
# are assigned at top level, which under `iex` means the *caller's own current scope* -- so they
# leak into, and stay in, the interactive session that ran the one-line form. Moving every one of
# those assignments inside `& { ... }` (with `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` as the first
# statement in the block, per the review) keeps them local to the block's own child scope; nothing
# escapes back to the caller, whether the caller is an interactive session (`iex`) or the top-level
# scope of a `-File` invocation (where the block's parent scope is the script scope, which is
# discarded when the script file itself finishes either way).
#
# The same condition also replaces every `exit N` with `throw`. `exit` (about_Language_Keywords:
# "Causes PowerShell to exit a script or a PowerShell instance") is a host/process-level operation:
# typed or evaluated in an interactive session, it closes that session, not just "this script" --
# there is no per-script `exit` in PowerShell the way there is no equivalent in, say, a piped-in
# shell script read by `sh -s` being any different from a saved one. `throw`, by contrast
# (about_Throw: "the throw keyword unwinds the entire call stack. Execution stops completely unless
# the error is caught by a try/catch block or trap statement") only unwinds the call stack -- it
# does not exit the host process on its own. Under `-File`, an uncaught throw still exits the host
# non-zero: about_Language_Keywords's own `exit` section states "If the script has no exit
# statement, the exit code is always 0 when the script completes without error or 1 when the script
# terminates from an unhandled exception" -- so `$LASTEXITCODE`/the process exit code keep working
# exactly as before for every existing test and every saved-file user. Under `iex` in an interactive
# session, the same uncaught throw is reported as an ordinary error at the top of the call stack and
# returns control to the prompt -- it does not invoke `exit`'s own process-level behavior, so the
# session survives. See the report for the citations and the child-session test that exercises this.
& {
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

# C3 (review 0.54.0-step-3-part-6a-review-v1): printed once near the start of every run so a CI log
# (or a user's own terminal) shows which engine actually executed this script, not just which engine
# launched it -- `scripts/windows-installer-test.ps1` relies on this line's own text, not merely on
# which engine ran the test script itself, since Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 are
# different hosts with no other obvious marker in this script's own stdout.
Write-Host "prikk-install: running under PowerShell $($PSVersionTable.PSVersion)"

# C2 (review 0.54.0-step-3-part-6a-review-v1): read/write HKCU\Environment's Path value through the
# raw registry API (Microsoft.Win32.RegistryKey), never through [Environment]::Get/SetEnvironmentVariable.
# `RegistryKey.GetValue`'s own documentation (the default overload, no options) states: "When the
# GetValue method retrieves expandable string values (RegistryValueKind.ExpandString), it expands
# environment strings using data from the local environment" -- confirmed from that page, not
# assumed -- and `Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable(string, string, EnvironmentVariableTarget)`'s
# own signature takes no `RegistryValueKind` parameter at all, so it cannot write back a value as
# `REG_EXPAND_SZ` even if that is what was there before; its own Remarks document only that it
# stores the User target "in the HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Environment key". The combination means a plain
# read-modify-write through `[Environment]::...` silently expands any `%VAR%`-style entry someone
# else added to that literal expansion it happened to have at read time, and silently downgrades the
# value's own registry kind from `REG_EXPAND_SZ` (`RegistryValueKind.ExpandString`, "a null-terminated
# string that contains unexpanded references to environment variables... equivalent to the Windows
# API registry data type REG_EXPAND_SZ" -- `RegistryValueKind`'s own documentation) to `REG_SZ`
# (`RegistryValueKind.String`) on write. `RegistryKey.GetValue(name, defaultValue, options)` with
# `RegistryValueOptions.DoNotExpandEnvironmentNames` is documented for exactly this: "you can specify
# ... DoNotExpandEnvironmentNames when retrieving a registry value of type
# RegistryValueKind.ExpandString to retrieve the string without expanding embedded environment
# variables" -- confirmed from that page's own Remarks, with a worked example showing the unexpanded
# read side by side with the expanded one.
function Get-RawUserPathEntry {
  $key = [Microsoft.Win32.Registry]::CurrentUser.OpenSubKey('Environment', $false)
  if ($null -eq $key) {
    return @{ Value = ""; Kind = [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryValueKind]::String }
  }
  try {
    $exists = $false
    foreach ($name in $key.GetValueNames()) {
      if ($name -eq 'Path') { $exists = $true; break }
    }
    if (-not $exists) {
      return @{ Value = ""; Kind = [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryValueKind]::String }
    }
    $kind = $key.GetValueKind('Path')
    $raw = $key.GetValue('Path', "", [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryValueOptions]::DoNotExpandEnvironmentNames)
    return @{ Value = [string]$raw; Kind = $kind }
  } finally {
    $key.Close()
  }
}

function Set-RawUserPathEntry([string]$Value, [Microsoft.Win32.RegistryValueKind]$Kind) {
  $key = [Microsoft.Win32.Registry]::CurrentUser.CreateSubKey('Environment')
  try {
    $key.SetValue('Path', $Value, $Kind)
  } finally {
    $key.Close()
  }
  Send-EnvironmentChangeBroadcast
}

# `Environment.SetEnvironmentVariable`'s own Remarks state: "If target is User or Machine, other
# applications are notified of the set operation by a Windows WM_SETTINGCHANGE message" -- that
# notification is a side effect of calling through `[Environment]::...`, not of the registry write
# itself, so a direct `RegistryKey.SetValue` call (above) does not send it; already-running processes
# (Explorer, other open shells) keep whatever PATH they read at their own startup until something
# broadcasts the change. `SendMessageTimeoutW`'s own Win32 signature (confirmed from its own
# documentation page): `LRESULT SendMessageTimeoutW(HWND hWnd, UINT Msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam,
# UINT fuFlags, UINT uTimeout, PDWORD_PTR lpdwResult)` -- broadcasting with `hWnd = HWND_BROADCAST`
# ("the message is sent to all top-level windows in the system"), `Msg = WM_SETTINGCHANGE`, and
# `lParam` pointing at the literal string "Environment" is the standard mechanism every real Windows
# installer (NSIS, WiX, ...) uses to announce an environment-variable change; this P/Invoke signature
# below marshals the Win32 `LPARAM` as a `string` (the common idiom for this exact call, since
# .NET/PowerShell interop marshals a `string` parameter to a native wide-character pointer by
# default) and the out `PDWORD_PTR` result as `UIntPtr` (pointer-sized, matching `DWORD_PTR`/`PDWORD_PTR`
# on both 32- and 64-bit).
#
# `Add-Type`'s own documentation: "Type names and namespaces must be unique within a session. You
# can't unload a type or change it ... Otherwise, the command fails" -- and, separately, "Beginning
# in PowerShell 7, Add-Type doesn't compile a type if a type with the same name already exists",
# which by its own wording implies Windows PowerShell 5.1 has no such built-in guard and fails on a
# second `Add-Type` for the same name. The `PSTypeName` existence check below is the standard
# PowerShell idiom to make `Add-Type` idempotent across repeat invocations in the same process (for
# example, a user who runs `irm ... | iex` more than once in the same interactive session) on both
# engines, since the one-line form's own session-leakage fix (the `& { }` wrapper, see above) does
# not and cannot un-load a type that a prior run already compiled into the process.
if (-not ([System.Management.Automation.PSTypeName]'PrikkInstaller.NativeMethods').Type) {
  Add-Type -Namespace PrikkInstaller -Name NativeMethods -MemberDefinition @'
[DllImport("user32.dll", SetLastError = true, CharSet = CharSet.Auto)]
public static extern IntPtr SendMessageTimeout(
    IntPtr hWnd,
    uint Msg,
    UIntPtr wParam,
    string lParam,
    uint fuFlags,
    uint uTimeout,
    out UIntPtr lpdwResult);
'@
}

function Send-EnvironmentChangeBroadcast {
  $hwndBroadcast = [IntPtr]0xffff
  $wmSettingChange = 0x1A
  $smtoAbortIfHung = 0x0002
  $result = [UIntPtr]::Zero
  [PrikkInstaller.NativeMethods]::SendMessageTimeout($hwndBroadcast, $wmSettingChange, [UIntPtr]::Zero, "Environment", $smtoAbortIfHung, 5000, [ref]$result) | Out-Null
}

# Windows PowerShell 5.1's default TLS negotiation can fall short of the TLS 1.2 GitHub's release
# CDN requires, depending on the machine's own .NET/OS defaults -- this is a documented Windows
# PowerShell 5.1 gotcha (Microsoft's TLS 1.2 guidance for older .NET Framework defaults), not
# something this script measured on a real 5.1 runtime (none is available in this project's own
# development environment -- see the report). PowerShell 7 (.NET) already defaults to TLS 1.2+ and
# tolerates this call as a harmless compatibility shim, so it is set unconditionally rather than
# conditioned on $PSVersionTable.
try {
  [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
} catch {
  # Best effort only; if the type or value does not exist on this runtime, downloading below will
  # fail with its own clear error instead.
}

$repo = "REPO_SLUG"
$version = if ($env:PRIKK_INSTALL_VERSION) { $env:PRIKK_INSTALL_VERSION } else { "latest" }
$installDir = if ($env:PRIKK_INSTALL_DIR) { $env:PRIKK_INSTALL_DIR } else { Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA "Programs\prikk" }

# 0.54.1: the architecture decision reads only Windows' own processor environment variables, never
# a .NET API. The previous round here used
# [System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::OSArchitecture, in a try, with
# $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE as the catch fallback -- on the reasoning that OSArchitecture is the
# OS's own real architecture while PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE alone can read a WOW64 process's own
# rewritten value instead. That reasoning was correct but the fallback was not: found on a real
# Windows 11 machine running Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.9711, the .NET property read raised no
# exception at all -- so the catch never ran -- yet still resolved to nothing. In Windows
# PowerShell, reading a member that does not resolve yields $null silently, and $null -eq X64 is
# false, so the try block "succeeded" with the installer refusing an ordinary x64 machine while
# printing an empty architecture value. GitHub's own windows-latest CI runner answers that same
# .NET expression correctly, which is why 13 passing CI runs under PowerShell 5.1 never caught
# this -- only a real end-user machine did.
#
# The lesson: a check whose failure is silent must not be what decides a refusal. Windows itself
# sets $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE for every process, and -- only for a 32-bit process running
# under WOW64 on 64-bit Windows -- also sets $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432 to the OS's own real
# architecture; that one is preferred when it is set, for the same WOW64 reason the old .NET call
# was preferred for. Neither variable's presence or value depends on any .NET runtime being
# loaded, so there is no fallback branch at all here: one read, used for both the decision and its
# own refusal message, never two separate reads that can disagree with each other.
$arch = if ($env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432) { $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432 } else { $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE }

if ($arch -eq "AMD64") {
  # Install the x64 build, as today.
} elseif ($arch -eq "ARM64") {
  Write-Host "prikk-install: this is ARM64 Windows; installing the x64 build, which runs under Windows' x64 emulation"
} else {
  $archDisplay = if ($arch) { $arch } else { "unknown" }
  Write-Host "prikk-install: download prikk-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip from the release page by hand," -ForegroundColor Yellow
  Write-Host "prikk-install: or run 'cargo install prikk'" -ForegroundColor Yellow
  throw "prikk-install: no prebuilt binary for Windows/$archDisplay (only x86_64 ships one)"
}
$target = "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"

if ($env:PRIKK_INSTALL_BASE_URL) {
  # Undocumented for ordinary use; exists so this script's own download-verify-extract logic can
  # be tested against a fixture server instead of the real release page -- the same purpose
  # install.sh's identical override serves.
  $baseUrl = $env:PRIKK_INSTALL_BASE_URL
} elseif ($version -eq "latest") {
  $baseUrl = "https://github.com/$repo/releases/latest/download"
} else {
  $baseUrl = "https://github.com/$repo/releases/download/$version"
}

$asset = "prikk-$target.zip"
$workDir = Join-Path ([System.IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) ("prikk-install-" + [System.IO.Path]::GetRandomFileName())
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $workDir | Out-Null

try {
  $assetPath = Join-Path $workDir $asset
  $checksumPath = Join-Path $workDir "$asset.sha256"

  Write-Host "prikk-install: downloading $asset ($version, $target)"
  # -UseBasicParsing: Windows PowerShell 5.1 otherwise tries to parse the response through the IE
  # engine, which can fail on a machine where Internet Explorer's first-run configuration was never
  # completed -- a documented 5.1 gotcha. PowerShell 7 accepts the same flag as a no-op.
  Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$baseUrl/$asset" -OutFile $assetPath -UseBasicParsing
  Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "$baseUrl/$asset.sha256" -OutFile $checksumPath -UseBasicParsing

  Write-Host "prikk-install: verifying checksum"
  # The .sha256 line shape was matched to sha256sum's own output on purpose (RFC 107 Stage 2):
  # lowercase hex, two spaces, no trailing newline -- so the comparison below is a plain string
  # compare of the hex, lowercased on both sides since Get-FileHash returns uppercase by default.
  $expectedLine = (Get-Content -Path $checksumPath -Raw).Trim()
  $expectedHash = ($expectedLine -split '\s+')[0].ToLowerInvariant()
  $actualHash = (Get-FileHash -Path $assetPath -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLowerInvariant()
  if ($actualHash -ne $expectedHash) {
    throw "prikk-install: checksum verification failed; refusing to install"
  }

  Write-Host "prikk-install: extracting"
  Expand-Archive -Path $assetPath -DestinationPath $workDir -Force

  $extractedExe = Join-Path $workDir "prikk.exe"
  if (-not (Test-Path -Path $extractedExe -PathType Leaf)) {
    throw "prikk-install: extracted archive did not contain a prikk.exe binary"
  }

  New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $installDir | Out-Null
  # Overwrites unconditionally, the same as install.sh's own `mv` over any existing binary at the
  # install path -- neither script checks for or prompts about an existing install first.
  Copy-Item -Path $extractedExe -Destination (Join-Path $installDir "prikk.exe") -Force

  Write-Host "prikk-install: installed to $installDir\prikk.exe"

  $markerPath = Join-Path $installDir "path-added-by-install.marker"
  $rawPath = Get-RawUserPathEntry
  $pathEntries = @()
  if ($rawPath.Value) {
    # Part 6a3 (review 0.54.0-step-3-part-6a2-review-v1, condition C1): wrapped in @(...). Without
    # it, a user PATH with exactly one entry made this pipeline unwrap to a bare string, not a
    # one-element array -- about_Arrays's own "array subexpression operator" section states plainly:
    # "The array sub-expression operator creates an array from the statements inside it. Whatever
    # the statement inside the operator produces, the operator places it in an array. Even if there
    # is zero or one object." The same page's own worked example shows this exact shape: piping a
    # one-match Where-Object result to a bare variable leaves `$result.GetType().FullName` as
    # `System.String`, not an array, and its own text says "If you want `$result` to be an array of
    # strings, you need to declare the variable as an array." $pathEntries then being a scalar made
    # `$pathEntries + $installDir` below (line ~267) a string concatenation with no separator instead
    # of an array append, corrupting a one-entry PATH into one merged entry.
    $pathEntries = @($rawPath.Value -split ';' | Where-Object { $_ -ne '' })
  }
  $alreadyOnPath = $pathEntries -contains $installDir

  if (-not $alreadyOnPath) {
    # User Path only, never the machine's -- writing the machine's PATH requires administrator
    # rights and would affect every account on the machine; install.sh has no such distinction to
    # mirror since a shell rc file is already per-user. $installDir is always a concrete, already-
    # resolved path (either $env:LOCALAPPDATA's own expanded value, or a literal override the caller
    # set in $env:PRIKK_INSTALL_DIR) -- comparing and appending it as a literal string against the
    # *unexpanded* existing entries above is correct either way: it never needs to match or produce
    # a %VAR%-style entry of its own.
    $newPath = ($pathEntries + $installDir) -join ';'
    # Part 6a3 (review 0.54.0-step-3-part-6a2-review-v1, condition C5): the marker is written BEFORE
    # the PATH registry write, not after. Today, a failure between the two leaves our entry in PATH
    # with no marker, so uninstall never removes it. Reversed, the worst case is a marker with no
    # entry, and uninstall then removes nothing, which is harmless. uninstall.ps1's own order (remove
    # the PATH entry first, then the marker) is already the safe one for the same reason, in reverse:
    # a failed uninstall can simply be re-run, so it is left unchanged.
    Set-Content -Path $markerPath -Value "This file records that install.ps1 added $installDir to this user's PATH.`r`nuninstall.ps1 reads it to decide whether to remove that PATH entry.`r`nDelete it only if you understand why." -NoNewline
    Set-RawUserPathEntry -Value $newPath -Kind $rawPath.Kind
    # install.sh does not prompt before appending to a shell rc file; this script follows the same
    # rule and does not prompt before this PATH change either -- see the report for the open
    # question of whether both should.
    Write-Host "prikk-install: added $installDir to your user PATH (open a new terminal for it to take effect)"
  } else {
    Write-Host "prikk-install: $installDir is already on your user PATH"
  }

  Write-Host "prikk-install: done. Run 'prikk --version' (in a new terminal, if PATH was just updated)."
  Write-Host "prikk-install: this checksum proves the download matches what the release page published;"
  Write-Host "prikk-install: it does not prove who published it. In v0 one maintainer key signs every release"
  Write-Host "prikk-install: tag; release-signers.toml is empty because no multi-signer policy exists yet."
} finally {
  Remove-Item -Path $workDir -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
}
}
